title: Autoon tehtiin vuosihuolto
subtitle: An annual service was done on the car

blocks.text: You can already say what things were (oli), and what didn't happen (ei toiminut). Now you need the verb shape that runs through almost every review describing actual work: the passive. This lets Finnish say 'a service was done', 'the part was changed', 'I was charged' — without ever naming who did it. It's everywhere in this corpus, and once you spot the pattern you'll never un-see it.

blocks.translation: An annual service was done on the car.

blocks.title: Why nobody is named
blocks.text: Notice: the reviewer never says who did the service. Not 'the mechanic did', not 'they did' — just tehtiin, 'was done'. Finnish uses this passive constantly, far more than English does, especially when describing a process rather than a person. It's the natural, neutral way to report 'this happened', and reviewers lean on it heavily.
Piece 1 — Tehtiin: the passive of tehdä

blocks.content: Tehdä means 'to do/make'. Its passive past form is {tehtiin|grammar|passive past|was done/was made} — 'was done'. You attach it to whatever got done: autoon tehtiin huolto (a service was done on the car), autoon tehtiin lommoja (dents were made on the car — from a bad review you'll recognise later).

items.en: An annual service was done on the car.

blocks.text: Piece 2 — Vaihdettiin and veloitettiin: parts and money

blocks.content: Two more passives you'll meet constantly: {vaihdettiin|grammar|passive past|was changed/replaced}, from vaihtaa (to change/replace) — used every time a part gets swapped. And {veloitettiin|grammar|passive past|was charged}, from veloittaa (to charge/bill) — used every time a reviewer reports what they paid.

blocks.title: One ending, dozens of verbs
blocks.text: Tehtiin, vaihdettiin, veloitettiin, sanottiin, soitettiin — all passive past, all built the same way: take the verb stem and add {-ttiin|grammar|suffix|passive past ending} or -tiin. No subject, no personal ending, just the action itself reported as having happened. Once you can hear this ending, you can identify a passive verb even if you don't know its exact meaning yet.

items.en: I was called the next day.
The car was fixed ahead of schedule.

lines.speaker: A
lines.en: What was done to the car?

lines.speaker: B
lines.fi: Autoon tehtiin vuosihuolto ja termostaatti vaihdettiin.
lines.en: An annual service was done on the car and the thermostat was changed.

lines.speaker: B
lines.fi: Minulta veloitettiin 161 euroa, mutta hinta-arvio piti paikkansa.
lines.en: I was charged 161 euros, but the price estimate was accurate.

blocks.title: Paul Noble Rule
blocks.text: You don't need to memorise every passive verb separately. Learn the shape -ttiin/-tiin once, and every new verb you meet that ends this way is instantly readable: korjattiin (fixed), katsottiin (looked at), annettiin (given). Pattern first, vocabulary second.

blocks.content: Tehtiin: TEH-tiin (long 'ii' at the end — hold it). Vaihdettiin: VAIH-det-tiin (the 'vaih' rhymes with English 'my', not 'vay'). Veloitettiin: VE-loi-tet-tiin (four syllables, stress stays on the first — Finnish never moves the stress no matter how long the word gets).

blocks.title: What you now own
items: tehtiin, vaihdettiin, veloitettiin — was done, was changed, was charged
the general -ttiin/-tiin passive past pattern, usable on new verbs you meet
vuosihuolto — annual service, another compound word built from parts you know
You can now describe what a shop did to a car without ever naming who did it
You can recognise a passive verb on sight, even one you've never seen before
